prompt.context: Our client, Shermer Pharma, is a venture backed start-up pharmaceutical company. Over the past 15 years, Shermer has been developing a molecule that has been approved by the FDA to cure Alzheimer's with 90% efficacy. Shermer's owners have hired us to determine how they should sell their product and whether it will be profitable.
prompt.question: 1) How should Shermer sell its product? 2) Will the product be profitable?

clarifying_info.a: A pill that cures Alzheimer's — an illness that currently has no treatment that cures or stops the progress of the disease. Alzheimer's is a degenerative, terminal disease that causes senility and dementia. 30 million people suffer worldwide.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the target customers (physicians, patients)?
clarifying_info.a: Sales would be focused on Neurologists and Geriatric psychiatrists, not the consumer of the product.

clarifying_info.q: Does Shermer have an existing Sales or Marketing organization?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has purely been a research firm to this point and has no Sales or Marketing organization.
Yes, FDA approval and all related regulatory steps have been completed.
We will not focus on competitive response during this case. Shermer is the only firm with a cure for this illness and will be for the next 5 years.

exhibits.title: Sales Force Options
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two sales force options: Develop Own Sales Force vs. Contract Sales Force. It includes rows for: Percent of visit focused on our product, Fully loaded annual cost of 1 sales rep, Cost per sales call, Total calls required, Total Sales Reps needed, and Total annual Selling Cost. Several cells are intentionally blank for the candidate to calculate.

exhibits.title: Annual Net Income
exhibits.shows: A 5-year P&L table with rows for Projected Market Penetration, Total Users, Total Gross Margin, Amortized R&D Costs, Selling Costs, G&A Costs, and Net Income. Market penetration rates are given for each year. Most value cells are blank for the candidate to fill in.

framework: Separate the two questions: (1) Sales channel strategy, (2) Profitability / break-even analysis
Sales channel: identify options — own sales force, contract sales, or sell the company — then compare costs and fit with Shermer's core competency (research, not commercialization)
Market sizing: estimate the US/global Alzheimer's patient population to anchor revenue projections (interviewee should size; answer is 5MM)
Profitability: build a 5-year P&L using market penetration rates, gross margin per user, amortized R&D, selling costs, and G&A
Recommendation: choose the sales channel, state whether the product is profitable by Year 5, and flag risks / next steps

questions.prompt: What are the options for how Shermer should sell its product, and which do you recommend?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies three options: (1) Build own sales force, (2) Use a contract sales organization, (3) Sell the company to a larger pharma firm that already has commercial capabilities. Candidate should note that Shermer's core competency is R&D, not commercialization, making options 2 or 3 most aligned. Qualitative points: contract sales reps split attention (50% on Shermer's product), own sales force requires building an entire organization from scratch, selling the company is cleanest but depends on owner willingness. Financial comparison requires Exhibit 1.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total annual selling cost for both sales force options. (Assume 100,000 total calls required for own sales force.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must fill in blank cells. Key insight: contract sales is cheaper ($12MM vs $17MM/year) despite needing more reps and calls, because the per-call cost is much lower. A strong candidate will also note the qualitative trade-off: for an extra $5MM per year, an own sales force provides 100% focus vs. 50% for contract.

math.setup: Own Sales Force: cost per call = $200k × 85 calls per rep / 100 calls per rep. Total calls = 100k. Contract: calls = 100k × 2 (because only 50% focused). Contract reps = 170.
steps: Contract — Total calls required: 100k × 2 = 200,000 (because each call is only 50% focused, need twice as many)
math.answer: Own sales force: $17MM/year. Contract sales: $12MM/year. Contract sales is $5MM cheaper annually.

questions.prompt: Size the Alzheimer's market (number of US patients who would use a cure).
questions.guidance: This is a market-sizing brain teaser. Candidate should walk through their logic (US population ~300MM, % over 65, incidence rate of Alzheimer's among elderly). The interviewer should let them attempt it, then provide the answer of 5MM at the end of the exercise.

math.setup: Estimate: US population ~300MM. ~15% over 65 = 45MM elderly. ~10-12% of people over 65 have Alzheimer's ≈ ~4-5MM. Answer to provide: 5MM.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 and assuming contract sales, build the 5-year P&L and determine whether the product is profitable. The firm requires R&D costs be recovered by Year 5. Use straight-line amortization and ignore taxes. Selling costs = $12MM/year (contract); G&A = $25MM/year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate each row year by year. Key insight: Year 1 is unprofitable (-$87MM) but the product is strongly profitable from Year 2 onwards, and cumulative profits far exceed R&D cost by Year 5. Strong candidates note the price ($1,000/year for a life-saving cure) appears underpriced relative to willingness-to-pay.

math.setup: Total Users = Market Penetration × 5MM. Total Gross Margin = Total Users × $1,000. Amortized R&D = $1.5B / 5 = $300MM/year. Net Income = Gross Margin − R&D Amortization − Selling Costs − G&A.
steps: Year 1: Users = 5%×5MM = 250k; Gross Margin = 250k×$1k = $250MM; R&D = $300MM; Selling = $12MM; G&A = $25MM; Net = $250MM−$300MM−$12MM−$25MM = −$87MM
math.answer: Year 1: −$87MM (loss). Year 2: +$163MM. Year 3: +$913MM. Year 4: +$1.663B. Year 5: +$2.663B. Product is profitable and R&D is fully recovered by Year 5.

brainstorming.prompt: What else should Shermer consider before launching with a contract sales organization?

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: $1,000/year appears underpriced for a life-saving, previously incurable disease — willingness-to-pay analysis warranted
Payer dynamics: insurance coverage, Medicare/Medicaid reimbursement rates
Potential for tiered pricing or outcomes-based contracts

categories.name: Contract sales force risks
ideas: 50% focus means less selling intensity per call vs. own reps
Risk of losing contract partner or renegotiating terms
Alignment of incentives between Shermer and contract partner
Knowledge transfer and product training quality

categories.name: Option to sell the company
ideas: Shermer's core competency is R&D, not commercialization — a larger pharma acquirer has ready sales infrastructure
Venture backers may prefer a liquidity event over building a commercial operation
Valuation upside: a breakthrough Alzheimer's drug would command a significant premium
Downside: loss of ownership and control by current founders/owners

categories.name: Post-launch monitoring
ideas: Long-term efficacy tracking to defend the 90% claim

recommendation: Shermer should use a contract sales force as the go-to-market channel — it is $5MM/year cheaper than building an own sales force ($12MM vs. $17MM) and avoids building a commercial organization from scratch

The product will be profitable: though Year 1 results in a $87MM loss, the product generates $163MM net income in Year 2 and cumulative profits are strongly positive by Year 5, fully recovering the $1.5B R&D investment
An alternative worth serious discussion is selling Shermer to a larger pharma company — this is arguably optimal given Shermer's R&D-only heritage, but depends on owner preference
risks: Contract sales force split focus (50%) may reduce commercial effectiveness relative to a dedicated team
Year 1 operating loss requires adequate financing runway
Price of $1,000/year may be unsustainable or may leave significant value on the table
If a competitor reaches the market sooner than the 5-year window, market share projections may be overstated
next_steps: Negotiate and finalize a contract with a specialty pharma contract sales organization
Develop a pricing and market access strategy, including payer and reimbursement analysis
Establish G&A and compliance infrastructure required to operate as a commercial-stage company
Monitor competitive pipeline closely and revisit the build-vs-buy-vs-sell decision annually
